4dcc8cdcc3d6.title: PROV-O QA/QC report
4dcc8cdcc3d6.content: The after-check for the agentic engine (issue #1180, step 5). The deterministic engine checks the ODRL policy before a task and refuses. An agent swarm acts first, so this report checks the same policy after the fact. It reads each workflow instance’s history, writes it as W3C PROV-O, and re-runs authorizeTask, the before-check, on every step. Because history records only a name, the actor is treated as asserted. Advisory. The owner chose advisory first (2026-09-23), so findings are reported here and do not fail the build. check:prov-qaqc fails only when these outputs are stale, when a prov:Activity does not validate against ProvActivitySchema, or on an internal error. unknown is never read as permit. Nothing is invented. An entry with no actor, or in a lane that binds no role, gets no prov:Activity, because the schema requires prov:agent and prov:hadRole. It gets a finding instead. Every entry is asserted, so that is not listed as a finding. prov:hadRole stays required. PROV-O makes it optional, and the owner decided on 2026-09-24 to keep it required here anyway (“Keep required”): a step in a lane that binds no role is reported as no-role, never logged without a role.

4e1386f96240.title: Requirements
4e1386f96240.content: What this harness promises, one page per shipped feature. A feature starts as a proposal in Proposals, where the initial analysis, the MVP and the options are argued. When the feature ships, its proposal is moved here and filed. Its front matter becomes a Requirement, and its body keeps the reasoning. The move uses git mv, so git log --follow walks a requirement back through the argument that produced it.

51e10165165a.title: What a page here must carry
51e10165165a.content: The front matter is checked by bun run cat check:requirements against the bootstrap schema, bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, and the slug is the file name. No two documents in either sub-graph share a slug, so a filed proposal can never land on an existing requirement. | title, description and actors: the roles it is about, by id. | status: in-force once filed. superseded requires supersededBy. | proposedIn: the proposal’s path before the move. | statements: each with a key, a label, a conformance level (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY or SHALL NOT) and the requirement sentence. A functional statement may add activity, capability (“I want”) and benefit (“so that”). A non-functional one may add a category. | . A test run names the statements it checks, in its requirements array (folio-test-run/v1), as req:<slug>#<key>.

b5e07d3fbbbb.title: How filing is organised
b5e07d3fbbbb.content: The assessment of open requirements standards is recorded in methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md (bean folio-assistant-1gf7), and the literature search, candidate methodologies, and proposed BPMN filing process (Process_RequirementsFiling, processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn) are recorded in methodologies/requirements-filing-and-organisation.md and Requirements filing and organisation (bean folio-assistant-qh1s, issue #1164): . | Flat physical paths, two-level semantic IDs (Doorstop + MADR): Every filed requirement lives at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> and statement keys req:<slug>#<key>. Physical files stay flat so git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md is 1:1 and check:requirements checks slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/. | Faceted organisation by canonical concern group (Volere + IREB CPRE): Filed in-force requirements are indexed on this page under the eight canonical concern groups declared in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct). | Three-axis bidirectional traceability (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 5.2.7 + IREB + W3C PROV-O): Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward links (beans, skills, processes, RequirementSet, and test/attestations/ + test/runs/). | Immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired): Filed requirements are never deleted with git rm. 25181208ce14.title: Four things, in order
25181208ce14.content: 1. The work plan is where you say what you are doing. Not a chat message, not a comment — beans, a committed store any session or agent can read. Claim before you work so a sibling session does not pick up the same item; a bean that turns out not to be wanted is scrapped, with its reasons, never deleted. cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh && export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" beans list # what is open beans create "<title>" # ...after checking the title does not exist beans <id> --status in-progress # claim it, visibly . 2. Make your first folio. This repository is the platform; your content lives in its own. One command scaffolds it — the manifests, the declaration, the agent files and the link back here: . bun run cat init-folio --help . Then Get started walks the first block through validate, render and review. 3. Know which kind of thing you are writing. A document is structured prose; a paper is that plus the block kinds whose assertion is a formal claim, backed by Lean and typeset through LaTeX. The choice decides which blocks are legal and which gates run: Content types. 4. The documentation you will never read. All of it — the authoring guides, the architecture, the publication workflow, the generated schema and skill reference. It is here, it is thorough, and the honest expectation is that you will arrive at it from a search engine at the exact moment something breaks. That is a fine way to use it. The three steps above are the ones worth reading now. When it is the machinery that has you puzzled rather than the authoring — who does a thing, under which process, using which skill — start at The platform. One sentence there carries the whole model, and every word in it is a separately declared object.

e2f034157352.title: What is folio-assistant?
e2f034157352.content: folio-assistant is the platform — it does not contain content. It provides the skills, schemas, tooling, and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that an LLM-driven agent uses to plan, author, validate, review, test, and publish a folio of content that lives in a separate repository. Separation of concerns. This documentation describes the formalism of the framework and how to use folio-assistant — deliberately kept separate from any specific content. Where content appears in these pages, it is purely illustrative (an example), never the canonical artifact. flowchart LR A[Author + LLM] -->|chat / MCP tools| B(folio-assistant) B --> C{Content adapter} C -->|paper| D[Lean + LaTeX repo] C -->|WHO SMART DAK| E[L2 BPMN / DMN / Excel] C -->|WHO SMART IG| F[L3 FHIR / FSH] B --> G[Skills + Schemas + RBAC] D & E & F --> H[Published site / PDF / IG] .

7e04979eb6d3.content: folio-assistant is pluggable — each content type is handled by a content adapter and a matching skill package. The currently supported types: . | Content type | Artifacts | Skill package | . | Scientific papers & books | Lean 4 formalization + LaTeX/Markdown | authoring-math | . | WHO SMART Guidelines DAKs | L2 artifacts — BPMN, DMN, Excel data dictionaries, personas | authoring-who-smart-guidelines | . | WHO SMART Implementation Guides | L3 FHIR resources, FSH, IG Publisher output | authoring-who-smart-guidelines | . | Others | Pluggable — add a new adapter + skill package | Adding a content type | . The cross-cutting content-lifecycle package (plan → author → validate → review → test → publish → feedback → retire) applies to every content type. The publication workflow models it properly — as BPMN swimlanes, with the roles, the HCI validation gate, and the shared work plan.

d446e8093e79.title: Who it is for
d446e8093e79.content: A reader who is not a Git user: a WHO technical working-group member, a country reviewer, or a paper’s co-author. They see a sentence they would change and want to propose it without leaving the page, without an account beyond GitHub, and without learning Markdown. The owner has low dexterity. Every control must be a large target, reachable by keyboard, and a choice rather than typing wherever possible.

c41c82dd3bd4.title: What they need to do
c41c82dd3bd4.content: . | Change the text in place. Use a small formatting toolbar, as in any word processor. | See what they changed while they change it. Track changes, with new text in green, underlined and removed text in red, struck through. Colour must never be the only channel: underline and strikethrough carry the meaning on their own. | Say why. A Why field in the dialog, whose text becomes the issue’s Why section, so the reviewer reads the reason next to the change. | Make the editor as big as they need. The dialog is resizable. | Submit. A prefilled GitHub issue opens, with the block, its source, the diff and the why. | . Owner, 2026-10-14, on the first build: “i thought there would be a small toolbar (bold, underline, etc.). also would expect it to be resizable. new things in green, underlined. deleted things in red/marktrhough. the github issue has a why… cant we preopulate that with a field “why” in the popup?” .

89379fbce81f.title: What it must show
89379fbce81f.content: . | The block’s name (its label, e.g. prose:about-this-draft), not its file path. | The editor, with: . | a toolbar: bold, italic, strikethrough, heading, bullet list, numbered list, link, inline code, undo and redo; | for a paper, also math, plus the raw-LaTeX toggle (owner: “both”); | the track changes. | . | Variables and checks: each `` with its current value, and any syntax error or reference warning, compact and secondary. | Why, a multi-line field. | Submit as an issue and Cancel. | A plain explanation when the visual editor cannot load, which then offers raw Markdown editing. | . A conflict in the asks . Markdown has no underline. An underline button would have to write HTML <u>, which the folio renderers do not all keep. An underline used for formatting would also be indistinguishable from the insertion mark. Both candidates therefore leave underline out of the toolbar and say so, offering bold, italic and strikethrough. This is for the owner to confirm.

7626e3352244.doc: SDLC Agentic Coverage: Mapping Folio-Assistant to the LMA State of the Art
7626e3352244.title: SDLC Agentic Coverage — Mapping Folio-Assistant to the State of the Art
7626e3352244.content: This architectural analysis cross-examines folio-assistant against the state of the art in Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent (LMA) systems for Software Engineering, synthesizing findings from the comprehensive 30-page systematic survey by He, Treude, and Lo (arXiv:2404.04834v4, 2025; ingested at library/arxiv-2404.04834v4). Corresponding methodology node: methodologies/sdlc-agentic-landscape.md.

37ceb1662df8.doc: SDLC Agentic Coverage: Mapping Folio-Assistant to the LMA State of the Art
37ceb1662df8.title: 1. Executive Summary
37ceb1662df8.content: He, Treude, and Lo categorize multi-agent software engineering into six core lifecycle phases: . | Requirements Engineering | Software Design | Code Generation & Implementation | Software Quality Assurance | Software Maintenance | Software Management & End-to-End Collaboration | . Folio-assistant implements 69 formal BPMN 2.0.2 executable processes and DMN 1.5 decision tables across six process groups (content/, kg/, library/, process/, sdlc/, ui/). Core Architectural Alignment . | Strengths: Folio-assistant exhibits exceptionally strong formalization in Requirements Engineering (CRDM suite), Software Design (BPMN/DMN models and MADR ADRs), Gated Quality Assurance (automated CI health, multi-voice adversarial reviews, signed QA attestations), and Management Coordination (git-backed bean claims and serialized merge queue). | Identified Gaps: As a document, guideline, and platform engineering harness, folio-assistant currently has gaps in post-deployment runtime monitoring (live APM/log diagnosis), continuous runtime telemetry feedback, and reverse-engineering of legacy codebases. | .

8d27bfd7a03a.doc: SDLC Agentic Coverage: Mapping Folio-Assistant to the LMA State of the Art
8d27bfd7a03a.title: 3. Detailed Gap Checklist
8d27bfd7a03a.content: Gap 1: Post-Deployment Monitoring & Production Observability . | The Survey Landscape: Advanced multi-agent systems such as RCAgent (Section 3.3) perform real-time root-cause analysis in production cloud environments. Agents collect streaming logs, monitor metrics, diagnose live anomalies, and issue incident reports. | Folio-Assistant Gaps: Folio-assistant monitors repository health and CI/build health (ci-health-watch.bpmn, repository-health-watch.bpmn), but has no active processes for monitoring runtime microservices, container health, or live production APIs. | Remediation Path: For deployments exposing HTTP/MCP servers or live guideline portals, introduce a processes/sdlc/runtime-telemetry-watch.bpmn process linked to Prometheus / OpenTelemetry alerts. | . Gap 2: Continuous Runtime Telemetry Ingestion Loop . | The Survey Landscape: LMA systems close the loop by automatically translating production crashes and operational telemetry into actionable bug tickets, triggering automated test synthesis and candidate patches. | Folio-Assistant Gaps: Folio-assistant’s beans work-tracking graph is updated by human developers, CI gate runs, and agent sessions, but lacks automated webhooks or synthetic telemetry ingestion. | Remediation Path: Define an ingest adapter that converts external incident payloads (e.g. Sentry, GitHub Security Alerts) into structured, pre-triaged beans with reproducible test fixtures. | . Gap 3: Legacy Software Reverse-Engineering . | The Survey Landscape: Modern LMA research emphasizes extracting architectural abstractions, class diagrams, and documentation from unstructured legacy codebases (100k+ lines of legacy C/Java) without tests. | Folio-Assistant Gaps: Folio-assistant is optimized for greenfield and forward-engineering (generating verified documents, Lean proofs, and structured code from formal schemas and CRDM requirements). It does not maintain reverse-engineering agents to infer schemas from raw legacy repositories. | Remediation Path: Implement a reverse-engineering skill in skills/sdlc/ that parses ASTs, detects implicit business rules, and outputs candidate DMN decision tables and BPMN process skeletons. | .

ad46444af480.doc: SDLC Agentic Coverage: Mapping Folio-Assistant to the LMA State of the Art
ad46444af480.title: 4. Architectural Lessons from Empirical Case Studies
ad46444af480.content: In Section 4, He et al. conduct case studies with ChatDev generating a Snake game and a Tetris game: . | Snake Game (Moderate Complexity): ChatDev succeeded on the 2nd attempt in 76 seconds at $0.019 cost, producing playable code and a manual. | Tetris Game (High State Complexity): ChatDev failed across the first 9 attempts. On the 10th attempt, it produced playable blocks but failed to implement line clearing, a core game requirement. | . Why Folio-Assistant Avoids This Trap . ChatDev’s failure on Tetris illustrates the inherent limit of unstructured multi-agent natural language chat for complex state machines: . | Unbounded Hallucination & Drift: Unconstrained role-playing agents agree on superficial interfaces while omitting subtle state transition invariants. | Folio-Assistant’s Defense: In folio-assistant, state machines and business rules are compiled into DMN decision tables (methodologies/dmn.md) and verified by deterministic gates or Lean 4 formalization. Rather than hoping an agent pair implements row-clearing correctly, the rule is captured as a deterministic decision table and verified against edge-case witnesses. | .
